query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing approximately 5 at.% vanadium into equal‐atomic BCC NbMoTaW will improve room‐temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance by modifying grain boundary chemistry and promoting controlled nano‐precipitate formation, while preserving its high‐temperature mechanical strength and BCC stability.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW exhibiting a single-phase BCC structure with excellent high-temperature strength (up to 1600 °C) but poor room-temperature ductility and signs of irradiation-induced instabilities (e.g., amorphization, blistering, and enhanced precipitation).
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition by adding approximately 5 at.% of a ductile element (vanadium) to the NbMoTaW matrix.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted over a broad temperature range—from room temperature to 1600 °C—and under controlled helium ion irradiation regimes that mimic reactor conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Segregation of vanadium to grain boundaries and the formation of controlled nanoscale precipitates that act both to improve grain boundary cohesion and serve as helium trapping sites.
generation.mechanism: The added vanadium is expected to segregate to grain boundaries, thereby enhancing their cohesion and mitigating brittleness at room temperature. Simultaneously, vanadium-related nano-features are anticipated to act as sinks for helium, reducing the formation of damaging bubbles and blisters under irradiation, all while maintaining the BCC phase that confers high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the vanadium-doped alloy should exhibit increased room-temperature ductility (e.g., higher uniform elongation and lower yield drop), reduced irradiation-induced defects (such as less blistering and amorphization), and comparable high-temperature mechanical performance within experimental variability.
generation.baseline: Untreated, equal-atomic NbMoTaW which shows excellent strength at temperatures up to 1600 °C but suffers from low room-temperature ductility and irradiation-induced phase instabilities.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to manifest across the temperature range from room temperature to 1600 °C and particularly under helium ion irradiation conditions representative of reactor environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the improvements in ductility and irradiation resistance is uncertain. Additionally, there is a risk that vanadium addition could inadvertently affect high-temperature phase stability or the nano-precipitate distribution if segregation is too extensive or uncontrolled.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloys: one of pure, equal-atomic NbMoTaW and one of NbMoTaW with an additional ~5 at.% of vanadium. Ensure both are processed under identical heat-treatment conditions to retain a single-phase BCC structure. Perform tensile tests at room temperature and at high temperatures up to 1600 °C, and subject both alloy variants to controlled helium ion irradiation experiments.
measurements: Stress-strain curves at room temperature and elevated temperatures (including yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation)

Microstructural characterization using SEM/TEM to assess grain boundary chemistry, nano-precipitate distribution, and irradiation-induced defects (e.g., helium bubble formation, blistering, amorphization)
Hardness measurements before and after irradiation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in room-temperature ductility or does not exhibit reduced irradiation-induced damage (e.g., similar or increased levels of blistering, amorphization, or precipitation) compared to the pure NbMoTaW baseline, or if its high-temperature mechanical properties are compromised, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . One of the most promising and progressive fields in modern material science is high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The first to propose HEAs’ concept was J.W. Yeh [ [1] ], but since then, it has changed rather significantly, especially during the last few years [ [2] ]. Due to their extremely high mechanical and physical properties, refractory HEAs are classified as a separate group of materials. Such alloying compositions mainly include elements from the IV, V, and VI columns of the periodic table with some additions of Al, Si, Ni, or Co [ [3] ].

First high-entropy equiatomic compositions based on refractory elements, such as NbMoTaW and NbMoTaWV, were obtained in prior research [ [4] , [5] ]. It was found that the alloys possess higher mechanical properties at higher temperatures in comparison to conventional superalloys, such as Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [6] ]. It was also determined that the addition of V increases the hardness significantly (up to 11.4 GPa at 1150 °C) [ [7] ] and yield strength σ 0.2 from 1058 MPa to 1246 MPa [ [5] ]. Other refractory HEAs have shown self-healing behavior and improved irradiation resistance, yet still suffer from irradiation-induced phase instabilities such as amorphization, blistering, and precipitation
frame.understanding: A promising intervention is to incorporate a minor addition of a ductile element (e.g., vanadium or chromium) into NbMoTaW. This addition is expected to promote beneficial grain boundary chemistry modifications—encouraging grain boundary segregation or controlled nano-precipitate formation—that can enhance room-temperature ductility and serve as helium sinks to mitigate irradiation damage, without disrupting the high-temperature BCC strength.
frame.experiment: Fabricate two samples: one of pure NbMoTaW and one doped with approximately 5 atomic percent of the ductile element (e.g., V). Perform standardized tensile tests at room temperature and high temperatures (up to 1600 °C) and subject both to controlled helium ion irradiation, monitoring for signs of blistering, amorphization, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation. The hypothesis would be falsified if the doped alloy does not show statistically significant improvements in room-temperature ductility and irradiation resistance, or if its high-temperature mechanical performance degrades relative to untreated NbMoTaW.

decision.trend: Initial studies on NbMoTaW confirmed its excellent high‑temperature strength in a single-phase BCC structure but unveiled its poor room-temperature ductility. Parallel work on other refractory high‑entropy alloys (HEAs) and BCC systems under irradiation has shown that while high‐temperature stability can be maintained, irradiation can trigger amorphization, helium‐induced blistering, and unwanted precipitation. Subsequent efforts have focused on tuning microstructures through processing (e.g., SLM or PBF) and modifying composition (via minor additions or promoting nano‐precipitation) to improve ductility and irradiation resistance. Although some alloys with controlled precipitate distributions or with elements such as V or Cr show moderated self-healing behavior and improved damage tolerance, the challenge remains to reconcile room-temperature ductility and irradiation resilience with the retained high-temperature and BCC structural stability.
decision.unsolved: How to simultaneously enhance the room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance of NbMoTaW without sacrificing its high-temperature mechanical performance and single‐phase BCC stability remains unresolved. In particular, the precise design rules for a minor alloying addition that can modify grain boundary chemistry to serve both as a ductility enhancer and a helium sink are still unclear.
decision.lever: Introduce a minor (≈5 at.%) addition of a ductile element such as vanadium into the equal‐atomic NbMoTaW matrix
decision.why: This approach follows the trend observed in refractory HEA research where slight compositional tuning has been used to adjust nano-precipitate formation and grain boundary chemistry. Vanadium is expected to segregate at grain boundaries to enhance room-temperature ductility and act as effective helium traps to mitigate irradiation-induced blistering and precipitation, while preserving the BCC structure and high-temperature strength. Prior work on irradiation-resistant tungsten-based HEAs and precipitation‐engineered refractory HEAs supports the potential of such targeted composition changes.
